source.title: Scaling Laws for Classical Machine Learning on Tabular Data: A Benchmark Study

record.tranche_reason: It tests analogous learning-curve power laws in classical tabular models, a different model and data setting from language-model pretraining. It does not test language-model loss scaling directly.
record.gate_note: The study reports test-error scaling with training-set size for classical tabular models, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. It does not sweep language-model parameters, tokens, or compute, test compute-optimal allocations, or evaluate downstream language-model performance. Its results are relevant as an extension to another setting and to the fit-dependence version.
record.test_reason: The study fits error(N)=aN^-b+c to learning curves of non-neural scikit-learn models (boosting, random forest, SVM, linear, ridge, lasso) on 18 small tabular datasets, varying only training-set size. Every version concerns language models (V1–V4, V6, V7) or neural models in other modalities and regimes (V5). None of its rows measures the same kind of system. Kaplan and Hoffmann appear only as background and in an exponent comparison in the Discussion. Its results are recorded under fits_no_version, not as tests. A reader who treats classical tabular learners as within V5 could instead read r1–r7 as a T3 extension; that call is the main judgment here.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that aN^-b+c fits 77.7% of classical tabular learning curves and that a family-level exponent gives approximate predictive compression, not universality: Lasso fails and Ridge is fragile. Fixed-seed re-implementations differ by CV(b)≈0.144. They add that tree ensembles dominate at full data and that the floor c, not the exponent, is the binding constraint in tabular ML.
record.recipe_differences: Uses classical scikit-learn model families on tabular classification and regression, varying training-set size and fitting test-error curves; it does not run neural language-model pretraining or measure cross-entropy against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Fit quality and exponent behavior vary by model family and dataset. Cross-replicator exponent spread remains with the seed fixed and is attributed to preprocessing, encoding, and missing-value handling. Ridge is fragile in leave-one-dataset-out tests; the five non-Lasso shared exponents change by less than 0.001 under the reported relaxed bounds.

fits_no_version.finding: The additive power law in training-set size fits classical tabular learners well for boosting, RF, SVM and linear models (87.9–94.8% with R2>0.8). It fits poorly for ridge (47.5%) and lasso (23.8%) under fixed regularisation; 77.7% overall.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning curves of classical (non-neural) models on tabular data follow error(N)=aN^-b+c, except for fixed-regularisation sparse or shrinkage linear models.

fits_no_version.finding: A single family-level exponent compresses cross-dataset curves for 4–5 families: in-sample R2 gap ≤0.011, LODO median gap 0.007–0.035. AIC favours dataset-specific exponents, and a permutation null shows the in-sample gap lacks specificity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-scaling exponents of classical tabular learners are approximately shared within a model family, but not universal across datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: With the seed fixed, independent re-implementations of one protocol give a mean CV(b)=0.144 in the fitted exponent, attributed to preprocessing, encoding and missing-value handling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitted scaling exponents carry roughly 14% implementation-induced spread across compliant re-implementations, at least in classical tabular learning curves.

record.problems: The study uses 18 small-to-medium tabular datasets, fixed hyperparameters, and a single split seed. Classification SVMs are capped at 10,000 rows. Replicators covered only three datasets each, and the authors describe the shared-exponent stress tests as descriptive; the in-sample R2-gap permutation null is not specific to a true shared exponent. The results do not directly test language models or language-model pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out.

untested.parts: No language models, no pretraining cross-entropy, no sweeps of parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to much larger LM runs. N* values beyond 10x extrapolation are flagged unreliable and are not LM runs.
No architecture-shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
No neural image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer settings. Only non-neural tabular learners vs. training-set size.
No LM exponents, compute-optimal splits, or comparison of published LM laws.

missing.what: Per-family exponent distributions (median b: RF 0.325, boosting 0.480, linear 0.830, ridge 1.654) and floors c. Needed alongside the fits_no_version rows and for the Discussion's comparison with Kaplan's 0.095.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 and V7 links rest on analogy. The systems are non-neural scikit-learn models on datasets up to 54k rows, and only training-set size is varied. V5 names neural models in other modalities or regimes; V7 names LM exponents and compute-optimal splits. Treating V5 as covering any learner would turn r1–r7 into a V5 test, with supports for boosting, RF, SVM and linear, and limits_scope for ridge and lasso. That reading is not adopted here. The paper's single author also cites several of his own unrelated works.

versions.untested_parts: No language models, held-out pretraining cross-entropy, or sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from small language-model runs to much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between language-model parameters and tokens.
No language-model architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Tests classical tabular models and training-set-size scaling only; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream language-model tasks or relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance.
Does not test language-model exponents or compute-optimal splits, nor whether published language-model laws disagree. Its fit-dependence evidence is for classical tabular learning curves.

rows.subject: Boosting
rows.operation_detail: Fit error(N) = aN^-b + c to seven nested training fractions per replicator, dataset, and model.
rows.measure: Percentage of per-replicator power-law fits with R2 > 0.8
rows.note: Classical tabular test error, not language-model pretraining loss.
rows.check: Classical gradient-boosting test error vs. training rows, not a neural model; linked to V5 wrongly.

rows.check: Classical random forest, not a neural model; V5 link removed.

rows.subject: Ridge
rows.operation_detail: Fit error(N) = aN^-b + c to seven nested training fractions per replicator, dataset, and model.
rows.measure: Percentage of per-replicator power-law fits with R2 > 0.8
rows.note: The study reports a pathology on california_housing where held-out RMSE briefly rises with N at intermediate fractions.
rows.check: Classical ridge fit quality; not V5 (wrong system) nor V7 (not LM exponents or published-law disagreement).

rows.subject: Lasso
rows.operation_detail: Fit error(N) = aN^-b + c to seven nested training fractions per replicator, dataset, and model.
rows.measure: Percentage of per-replicator power-law fits with R2 > 0.8
rows.note: The authors call Lasso a negative control and report that it can shrink all coefficients to zero at small N, leaving error flat and incompatible with monotone power-law decay.
rows.check: The authors' own Lasso negative control on classical models; not a test of any version.

rows.subject: all six classical model families
rows.operation_detail: Fit additive power laws to per-replicator tabular test-error curves.
rows.measure: Share of all fits exceeding the stated R2 threshold
rows.note: Aggregate reported by the study across model families and datasets.
rows.check: Aggregate fit rate over classical tabular models; not a neural or LM system.

rows.subject: Boosting
rows.operation_detail: Compare a shared exponent across datasets with an unconstrained fit using dataset-specific exponents.
rows.measure: Shared-exponent fit R2; unconstrained fit R2; R2 gap; ∆AIC
rows.value: Shared fit R2 0.992; R2 gap 0.002; ∆AIC +65 to +908 across families
rows.note: The small R2 gap indicates approximate compression, while AIC favors the fit with dataset-specific exponents.
rows.check: Shared-exponent compression across tabular datasets for classical boosting. It does not bear on LM exponents or compute-optimal splits (V7) or neural modalities (V5).

rows.measure: Shared-exponent fit R2; unconstrained fit R2; R2 gap
rows.note: The study reports AIC favors unconstrained fits on every family.
rows.check: Same as r8, for random forest.

rows.subject: Ridge
rows.operation_detail: Compare a shared exponent across datasets with an unconstrained fit using dataset-specific exponents.

rows.subject: Lasso
rows.operation_detail: Compare a shared exponent across datasets with an unconstrained fit using dataset-specific exponents.
rows.measure: Shared-exponent fit R2; unconstrained fit R2; R2 gap
rows.note: The authors say the confidence interval crosses zero and treat Lasso as a negative control demonstrating that a small gap alone is insufficient evidence for shared-exponent structure.
rows.check: Lasso negative control (CI crosses zero); not a version test.

rows.subject: Boosting
rows.operation_detail: Leave-one-dataset-out prediction using a shared exponent fitted on the remaining datasets.
rows.measure: Median held-out R2 gap between shared-exponent and unconstrained fits
rows.uncertainty: Fraction of folds within a 0.05 gap: 83.3%; shared-exponent CV across folds: 0.036–0.085 for the four well-behaved families
rows.note: The held-out result supports predictive compression, not exact equality of exponents.
rows.check: Leave-one-dataset-out transfer of a shared exponent in classical models; not LM fit dependence.

rows.uncertainty: Fraction of folds within a 0.05 gap: 75.0%

rows.check: Lasso LODO result, which the authors call meaningless; control only.

rows.subject: all model families with at least 5 replicators per cell
rows.operation_detail: Measure across-replicator coefficient of variation in fitted exponent b with the random seed fixed.
rows.measure: Unweighted mean CV(b) across replicators
rows.note: The authors attribute the spread to unconstrained implementation details such as preprocessing, encoding, and missing-value handling, not seed variance.
rows.check: Cross-replicator CV(b)=0.144 in classical tabular fits. Analogous to fit dependence, but not LM exponents or published LM laws.

rows.subject: all five non-Lasso model families
rows.operation_detail: Refit shared-exponent joint models with relaxed exponent and floor bounds.
rows.measure: Change in shared exponents after relaxing bounds
rows.value: All five non-Lasso shared exponents unchanged to within 0.001
rows.note: This robustness check did not find sensitivity of those shared-exponent estimates to these bound changes.
rows.check: Bound-sensitivity check on the study's own fitting method; a robustness check, not a version result. 'Absent' is not a meaningful state here.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Classical tabular models, especially Boosting, RandomForest, SVM, and LinearModel
reader_labels.reason: Power-law fits exceeded R2 > 0.8 in 87.9–94.8% of per-replicator curves for these families (r1–r4); the study also reports a 77.7% rate overall (r7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Lasso and Ridge in the tested tabular settings
reader_labels.reason: Fit quality was much poorer for these families, and the paper describes flat Lasso errors and a Ridge error increase that the fitted power-law form cannot represent (r5–r6).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Cross-dataset and cross-replicator fits for classical tabular models
reader_labels.reason: Dataset-specific exponents improve AIC for every family, LODO transfer varies by family, and fixed-seed implementation differences produce mean CV(b) = 0.144 (r8–r20).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Shared-exponent compression across datasets for the robust model families
reader_labels.reason: Despite AIC favoring unconstrained fits, shared-exponent R2 gaps are small for five families, and relaxed bounds barely change their estimates; this supports approximate compression rather than universal equality or strong general sensitivity to those bounds (r8–r12, r21).
